thread.title: After GM cuts, Wall Street cheer turns to auto-bubble fear

author: kopitiambot.com
title: After GM cuts, Wall Street cheer turns to auto-bubble fear
text:
(Source: marketwatch.com )
While the tech sector has gripped us lately, autos are stealing some limelight after GM announced plant closures and job losses on Monday.
Shares initially got a boost on the theory that cost cuts boost profits. But the mood could yet turn less positive for the sector as a whole.
That brings us to our call of the day , from Clarity Financial analyst Jesse Colombo, who sees trouble ahead for the auto sector. “Rising interest rates are threatening U.S. automobile sales and loan bubble and will eventually cause its popping,” he warned in a blog post .
“While GM’s CEO Mary Barra is spinning this move as a positive, I am highly suspicious because it is taking place at the same time that global auto sales are plunging,” explains Colombo, who warned about another bubble-soon-to-burst linked to household wealth and easy Fed policy, in October. Here’s his chart:
Colombo
Colombo delivered a similar warning a year ago when Ford announced investments in Michigan, and he notes that auto maker has also recently announced an $11 billion restructuring.
Since 2010, total outstanding U.S. auto loans are up $445 billion or 64% to over $1.1 trillion as Americans used record low interest rates to finance new cars, adds Colombo. “Low interest rates lead to borrowing booms that end when interest rates go back up, which is what has been happening over the past few years,” he warns.
Last word goes to Wolf Richter at the Wolf Street blog, who says GM’s plans will cost $3.8 billion, much of which will have to be borrowed. And that is because the auto maker “blew, wasted, and annihilated $13.9 billion in cash on share buybacks over the past four years,” he says, providing this chart:
To add insult to injury, GM’s shares fell 10% during that four-year period, even if they got a bump on Monday, Richter points out. You can read his full rant here .

The stat
Epic Games
200 million — that is the latest tally on those playing the wildly popular Fortnite shooting game, which is up 60% from a June update, and five times higher than in January.
Byron Lotter, money manager at Vestact notes that Fortnite owner, Epic Games, raised funds in October, that value the business at $15 billion. “That makes Tencent’s stake worth $6bn, bigger than Gowthpoint, Aspen and Woolworths,” said Lotter, in a note to clients.. Hong-Kong-based Tencent
0700, +1.95%
owns a 40% stake in the Epic Games.
